qs.q: A black grape is picked with unripe tannins. Which fault is most likely in the wine?
o: Bitterness
Excessive sweetness
Dried-fruit aromas
Overly deep colour
qs.e: During ripening, along with sugar and flavours, the tannins in black grape skins also ripen. Tannins shape the mouthfeel of red wines, but unripe tannins taste bitter. So the grower must time the harvest by checking not just the sugar level but also how ripe the tannins are.

qs.q: Why may grapes fail to ripen in a very hot summer with no rain?
o: Short of water, the vine shuts down to protect itself
The heat kills the yeasts on the skins and stops photosynthesis
The grapes take up too much water from the roots
The leaves fall straight after flowering
qs.e: High temperatures usually come with little rain, and in the worst cases the vine can die. Irrigation helps, but in these conditions there is often no water to use. Yeasts belong to fermentation in the winery, not ripening in the vineyard.

qs.q: Why is the vintage especially useful for expensive wines from prestigious regions with variable weather?
o: Each year's weather can greatly affect grape quality
It shows which grape was used
It reveals whether the wine is organic
It proves the wine always has the same style, whatever the year's weather
qs.e: A cool or rainy year can produce a wine different from what you expect. Knowing it helps you decide if the price is justified and when to drink the wine. The last option says the opposite: variability is exactly why the vintage matters.

qs.q: Which statement about maturing rosé wines is correct?
o: They are rarely stored or matured in oak
They are always matured in new barriques
They must age for at least five years
They stay on the skins for months during maturation to deepen the colour
qs.e: The rosé style relies on fresh fruit, which oak flavours would mask. Skin contact lasts only a few hours; months of maceration would make a red. There is no minimum ageing requirement for rosé.

qs.q: What are the two ways an oak barrel influences wine style?
o: Adding flavour and allowing oxygen contact
Raising alcohol and acidity
Adding sugar and tannin
Filtering the wine and clarifying it
qs.e: Barrels are watertight but not airtight. They therefore work in two ways: they add flavours such as vanilla, coconut or spice directly, especially when new, and they let a little oxygen interact with the wine, developing caramel and nut notes and softening red wine tannins. They do not raise alcohol, acidity or sugar.

qs.q: What does the term unoaked on a Chardonnay label tell you?
o: The wine has had no oak treatment
The wine was made from late-picked grapes
The wine is blended with Semillon
The wine has been acidified
qs.e: Some producers want a pure-fruited Chardonnay: they use inert vessels and sometimes avoid malolactic conversion and lees. To tell buyers, they may print unoaked or unwooded on the label. The term says nothing about harvest timing, blending or acidification. It is a simple way to guide people looking for a fresh, fruit-led style.

qs.q: Which grape is Sauvignon Blanc often blended with?
o: Semillon
Chardonnay
Viognier
Pinot Gris
qs.e: Sauvignon Blanc is mainly a single-varietal wine, but when blended its typical partner is Semillon: in Bordeaux (Bordeaux AOC, Graves, Pessac-Léognan) and in Australia (Margaret River, Adelaide Hills). Semillon adds body and helps the wine age. Sauvignon, for its part, brings acidity and herbaceous aromas to the blend.

qs.q: Why can Riesling make outstanding wines at every sweetness level?
o: High natural acidity and susceptibility to botrytis
Thick skins and high tannins
Low acidity and high alcohol
Fast ripening and high yields
qs.e: Riesling has high natural acidity that persists even when the grapes are very ripe. That acidity keeps dry wines fresh and balances the sugar in sweet wines perfectly. The grape is also susceptible to botrytis, which concentrates sugars, acidity and flavours and allows great sweet wines such as Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese.

qs.q: How is light Italian Pinot Grigio usually fermented?
o: Almost always to dryness
Stopped early to leave medium sweetness
In new barrels with long lees ageing and full malolactic
With sweet juice added after fermentation
qs.e: Light Pinot Grigio is fermented dry in inert vessels to keep its simple pear and lemon fruit. Stopping fermentation to keep sweetness is a choice some producers of the rich style make. New oak and added juice are not part of this style.

qs.q: Which South African region, cooled by strong southerly breezes, is known for Pinot Noir?
o: Walker Bay
Casablanca Valley
Yarra Valley
Martinborough
qs.e: In South Africa, Pinot Noir is focused on the coolest coastal regions. In Walker Bay, strong southerly sea breezes keep the grapes cool and encourage vibrant red fruit; a number of very good and outstanding wines are made here. Casablanca Valley is in Chile, Yarra Valley in Australia and Martinborough in New Zealand.

qs.q: Pessac-Léognan AOC lies within which area?
o: Graves
Haut-Médoc
Saint-Émilion
Pomerol
qs.e: Graves AOC lies south of the city of Bordeaux, on the Left Bank, and includes Pessac-Léognan AOC. As in the Haut-Médoc, Cabernet Sauvignon is usually the leading grape in the blend, supported by Merlot. Saint-Émilion and Pomerol are on the Right Bank instead.

qs.q: A Merlot has medium to full body with cooked blackberry and black plum. What grapes was it most likely made from?
o: Riper grapes, from a warm climate or later harvest
Just-ripe grapes, picked early
Grapes frozen on the vine
Grapes affected by noble rot
qs.e: The ripe style comes easily in warm climates, or by picking later in a moderate one. Just-ripe grapes give light to medium body, strawberry, red plum and green bell pepper. Frozen or botrytised grapes are for sweet wines.

qs.q: Why can the finest Syrahs age for a decade or more?
o: They have intense flavours and firm tannins
They have lots of residual sugar
They are bottled with no oak maturation
They have little alcohol and acidity
qs.e: With time, dried fruit, leather, meat and earth emerge. Syrahs are dry wines, oak maturation is in fact common, and low acidity and alcohol would not help ageing.

qs.q: Some Bordeaux classifications have not been updated for a long time. How should they be viewed?
o: Still a strong indication of quality
They no longer mean anything and have been abolished
They only mark simple wines for drinking young
They cover only the sweet wines of the Sauternes area
qs.e: Classified wines, which may state Grand Cru Classé or Cru Classé, are among Bordeaux's most expensive and sought-after and age for years or decades. They are neither simple wines nor only sweet ones.

qs.q: What style do Grenache rosés usually have?
o: Dry to medium-sweet, drunk chilled while young
Always very sweet, to be cellared for years
Dry and tannic, aged for a long time in new barrels before sale
Sparkling, with a second fermentation in bottle
qs.e: They are made with a short skin maceration, which gives colour but little tannin. Their strength is fresh fruit, so they are not aged or kept long in new oak. Bubbles are not part of this style.

qs.q: Compared with the wider Chianti DOCG, Chianti Classico DOCG vineyards:
o: Sit higher and enjoy a long ripening season
Lie on the plains and ripen very quickly
Lie on the coast and make sweet wines
Use only grapes dried indoors
qs.e: Chianti DOCG covers a wide area of varied quality, often simple, inexpensive wines. Chianti Classico DOCG, higher up, gives Sangiovese a long ripening season: the result is a medium-bodied wine with pronounced red fruit and dried herbs, often matured in oak.

qs.q: Which description matches a typical Malbec?
o: Deep colour, full body, high tannin, black fruit
Pale colour, light body, low tannin, red fruit
Medium colour, medium body, medium tannin, citrus
Pale colour, full body, low tannin, strawberry
qs.e: Argentine Malbec is typically deeply coloured, full-bodied and high in tannin, with black fruit such as blackberry and black plum. It is often single-varietal but also blended with Cabernet Sauvignon and/or Merlot. Pale, light profiles with red fruit describe Gamay instead; strawberry is typical of Grenache and Pinotage.

qs.q: Which is the most important grape in Soave DOC?
o: Garganega
Cortese
Corvina
Fiano
qs.e: Soave and Valpolicella are both in the Veneto, but Soave is a white based on Garganega, while Valpolicella is a red based on Corvina. Cortese belongs to Gavi in Piemonte and Fiano to Campania. The name Soave on the label refers to the area, not the grape.

qs.q: Why do some Nebbiolo producers choose new barrels instead of old ones?
o: To add new-oak aromas to the wine
Because Barolo law requires only new barrels
To raise the tannins, which are too low in Nebbiolo
To make the wine sweet
qs.e: Nebbiolo is often aged for a long time in oak to soften its already high tannins. The choice between old and new oak is free and depends on the style wanted. Oak adds no sugar.

qs.q: How is a Hunter Valley Semillon usually made and bottled?
o: In inert vessels, bottled young
In new oak barrels, bottled after two years
In a solera of old casks, then fortified
With a second fermentation in bottle and long lees contact
qs.e: The complex honey and nut flavours come only after several years in bottle, not from oak. Long barrel ageing applies to some Barossa Semillons. Solera, fortification and second fermentation belong to Sherry and sparkling wine.

qs.q: Which three grapes are typical of Champagne?
o: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier
Chardonnay, Glera and Moscato
Chenin Blanc, Pinot Noir and Meunier
Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot and Chardonnay
qs.e: In Champagne the base wine is usually a blend of three grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier. The region's cool climate gives grapes with high acidity and little sugar, perfect for a light, fresh base wine. Glera and Moscato are the grapes of Prosecco and Asti, while Chenin Blanc appears in some Cap Classique wines.

qs.q: In an Amontillado, which note comes from the time under flor?
o: Bread dough
Walnut
Caramel
Dried fig, molasses and liquorice
qs.e: Amontillado combines two worlds: bread dough from flor, then walnut and caramel from oxidation after refortification. Fig, molasses and liquorice are notes of sweet PX, not dry Amontillado.

qs.q: Why does a mature Vintage Port need decanting?
o: A thick deposit forms in the bottle
To let the added spirit evaporate
To warm it to room temperature
To remove bubbles from a second fermentation in bottle
qs.e: Vintage spends little time in cask and decades in bottle, where it throws sediment. Ruby and tawny styles are bottled ready to drink and normally have none. Decanting does not remove alcohol or warm the wine.

qs.q: At what temperature should a sweet wine such as Sauternes be served?
o: 6–8 °C, well chilled
10–13 °C, lightly chilled
13–18 °C, chilled or room temperature
15–18 °C, room temperature
qs.e: Sweet wines such as Sauternes are among the coldest-served wines, at 6–8 °C. Sparkling wines are also served well chilled, at 6–10 °C. 10–13 °C suits full-bodied whites such as an oaked Chardonnay; 13–18 °C suits light-bodied reds; 15–18 °C suits medium- and full-bodied reds.

qs.q: Which of these does NOT belong in a good tasting environment?
o: Scented candles on the table
Good lighting to judge appearance
Enough space to lay out glasses and take notes comfortably
Spittoons available
qs.e: Light, space and spittoons all help. A scent in the air, such as from candles, confuses the nose and makes the wine's aromas hard to identify.
